title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the impact of cocaine use on cognitive inhibition

claims.statement: In cross-sectional studies, people with cocaine dependence or cocaine use disorder score lower on average than comparison groups who do not use cocaine on several tests of memory, attention, stopping a started response and decision making, but the size of the difference is uncertain, the studies disagree, and none of the designs can show that cocaine caused it or that scores recover with time off cocaine. Four reviews, all rated critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2, cover overlapping literatures. A 2005 effect-size review of 15 studies (481 people who used cocaine, 586 comparison participants, 1987–2002) gives a median difference of about 0.35 standard deviations across 140 test measures, 93 of them from a single study; on the measures used in several studies the differences are smaller and mixed (Trail Making B 0.49 across 9 estimates, Trail Making A 0.19 across 10, Stroop colour-word interference −0.11 across 7), while the largest values, around 1 standard deviation, come from single small studies, the largest of them on a test the cocaine group did better on. A 2013 review pooled three to nine cross-sectional studies per outcome, dropping studies that raised heterogeneity in four of eight pools, and reported standardized differences of 0.24 to 1.22, all in the direction of poorer performance; its heterogeneity statistics are not printed. A 2026 meta-analysis of 20 studies of laboratory inhibition tasks (542 people with cocaine use disorder, 656 comparison participants) gives g = 0.65 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.03) with a 95% prediction interval of −0.95 to 2.26, significant funnel asymmetry (Egger p = .008), and two small studies whose effects (3.1 to 4.9) lie far outside the rest; without those two the first reader's recalculation gives 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62) with the asymmetry gone. A 2018 critical review of 47 studies argues the opposite reading, that the evidence does not support broad deficits, mainly because most studies did not compare performance with test norms, did not match groups on age or education and did not control for other drug use; its own table nonetheless lists poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one area in 19 of the 21 studies with a comparison group (the first reader's count), and in the one study using age-adjusted scores the cocaine group's impairment was mild, less than 1 standard deviation below the comparison mean. Where abstinence is reported it varies from current use to about three years, and in both the 2013 and 2018 reviews a substantial minority of studies tested people within 72 hours of last use or with positive urine tests; no review could analyse whether scores differ by time since last use, and the 2026 meta-analysis, whose own criterion was at most two months, included five studies with average abstinence of 152 to 335 days. In almost every study the cocaine groups also used alcohol, cannabis or other drugs (6.7% to 100% alcohol and 12.5% to 80% cannabis across the 2026 review's tables), comparison groups often had more education and were younger, and nothing was adjusted for; the one study read in full that followed people through four weeks of enforced abstinence had no comparison group at all, and within it heavier reported drinking and heavier reported cocaine use predicted different tests (Bolla et al., 2000). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Positive values mean poorer performance in the cocaine group unless stated. Jovanovski et al. (2005; 15 studies, 481 against 586): median absolute difference 0.35 across 140 measures (93 from one study); multi-study measures Trail Making B 0.49 (9 estimates), Trail Making A 0.19 (10), Stroop colour-word interference −0.11 (7), WAIS-R Digit Symbol −0.49 (6), Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall −0.45 (6), WAIS-R Arithmetic −0.66 (5); the largest single-study values about 1, including 1.09 on a test the cocaine group did better on. Spronk et al. (2013), pooled standardized differences: sustained attention −1.22 (−1.58 to −0.85), failed inhibitions 0.64 (0.44 to 0.84, 8 to 9 studies), stop-signal reaction time 0.50 (0.11 to 0.90, 3), immediate recall −0.46 (−0.70 to −0.23, 8), perseverative errors 0.37 (0.17 to 0.57, 5), reward-based decision making 0.53 (0.32 to 0.75, 7), psychomotor motor responses 0.75 (0.46 to 1.04, 3), psychomotor response time −0.24 (−0.47 to −0.02, 6); studies were dropped for heterogeneity in four of these pools and no I² is printed. López-Martín et al. (2026; 20 studies, 23 effects): g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03), I² 83.6%, prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26, leave-one-out 0.51 to 0.72, Egger p = .008; the first reader's recalculation without two outlying small studies gives 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62), I² about 65%, Egger p = 0.31; no moderator (sex, age, years of use, days of abstinence, clinical against community sample) was significant; 16 of 27 individual comparisons were significant, including 4 of 10 stop-signal studies. Frazer et al. (2018): no pooling; 19 of 21 studies with a comparison group list poorer performance in at least one area (first reader's count); 13 of 22 did not interpret results against norms, 6 of 22 did not match on education, 8 of 22 did not control for other drug use; 11 of 14 functional-imaging studies found no group difference on their cognitive task. Bolla et al. (2000; 56 people, no comparison group): drug-dose terms account for about 8% to 24% of the residual variance in the tests they predict (study card's calculation from the printed F statistics).
